title: A Copper Buddha and a Golden Vishnu

title_i18n.en: A Copper Buddha and a Golden Vishnu

subtitle: In the laughing city of kings, copper and gold shine on different gods from the same throne
region: Parihasapura, Kashmir monasteries and temple networks
moral: A wise state can protect more than one sacred path.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini, Book IV, Parihasapura passages; Stein trans., Vol. 1 (1900)
sources.note: Primary account of Buddhist and Vaishnava buildings in the same royal complex.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyouji, Kasmira chapter; Beal trans. (1884), pp. 147-160
sources.note: Earlier snapshot of Kashmir's mixed Buddhist and Deva-temple landscape.

sources.citation: Alexis Sanderson, The Saiva Age (2009), pp. 41-80; Hermann Goetz (1969), pp. 11-16
sources.note: Context for early medieval Kashmir's religious plurality and art.

panels.shot: wide aerial over the ruins of Parihasapura fading into a glowing reconstruction

dialogue.text: In Parihasapura, the Karkota kings raised a copper Buddha and a golden Vishnu in one royal city. How did one throne bind many faiths to its power?

panels.shot: slow push-in from misty Himalayan ridges to the valley of Kashmir

dialogue.text: When Xuanzang crossed into Kasmira, he saw Buddhist monasteries and Deva temples sharing the same valley. Centuries later, Karkota rulers turned that mixed sacred land into an instrument of rule.

panels.shot: documentary montage wide shot of coins and sculptures laid out on a table

dialogue.text: Coins from their mint show tridents, discus, and auspicious symbols. Stone and bronze images echo Buddhist calm, Saiva power, Vaishnava grace, and older Iranian-Kushan forms. The court spoke many sacred languages.

panels.shot: low-angle wide as architect-priests present plans before the throne

dialogue.speaker: Parihasapura Patron
dialogue.text: A city of laughter, yes. But also a city of bonds. Show me how stone can bind hearts.

panels.shot: sweeping bird’s-eye over the planned city of Parihasapura

dialogue.text: Kalhana’s chronicle names this new royal city Parihasapura, the City of Laughter. Here, Karkota patronage set Buddhist and Vaishnava monuments side by side, in one designed landscape of power.

panels.shot: epic vertical shot up along scaffolding of the copper Buddha

dialogue.text: Kalhana speaks of an immense copper Buddha raised in Parihasapura, so large that later scholars compared it to Bamiyan. The chronicles remember its size, not its end.

panels.shot: medium shot at ground level as molten copper is poured into molds

dialogue.text: Casting such a Buddha demanded wealth, metal, labor, and organized craft. Patronage bound monasteries to the throne, as royal favor made their teaching and landholdings secure.

panels.shot: wide symmetrical shot of the copper Buddha facing the Vishnu temple across a plaza

dialogue.text: Across the same royal space, Kalhana places a great Vishnu temple. In Parihasapura, Buddha and Vishnu did not compete in stone. They faced each other as twin pillars of one imperial city.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot inside the Vishnu temple sanctum

dialogue.text: The golden Vishnu drew Brahmin lineages and temple networks to Parihasapura. Land grants, rituals, and honor tied them to the crown, as firmly as copper bound the Buddha’s form.

panels.shot: cross-cut split composition between a monastic assembly and a Brahmin sabha

dialogue.text: This was not modern, slogan-ready tolerance. It was statecraft. By funding monasteries and temples together, Karkota rulers drew monastic scholars, Brahmin jurists, and local elites into their circle.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Patron’s contemplative face at twilight between monuments

dialogue.text: Kalhana lists more shrines and halls in Parihasapura. Saiva symbols, Vaishnava images, Buddhist forms, older motifs—all met here. The city was a map of the empire’s religious landscape.

panels.shot: documentary-style still of sandstone reliefs and pillars being examined

dialogue.text: Art historians trace Kushan, Iranian, and Indian patterns in early medieval Kashmir’s sculpture. The Karkota court did not erase older strands. It wove them into new, royal-sponsored sanctuaries.

panels.shot: medium shot in royal office as land grant charters are sealed

dialogue.text: Grants to Buddhist foundations and to Brahmin-led temples secured loyalty. Land, tax exemptions, and ritual prestige turned religious institutions into supporting pillars of Karkota governance.

panels.shot: soft focus montage of rituals at both monuments

dialogue.text: Day after day, different rituals rose from the same city. Chanting in Pali or Sanskrit, hymns to Vishnu or praises of Buddha—all unfolded under one dynastic shadow.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of the city slowly fading over centuries

dialogue.text: Later centuries brought new rulers, new priorities, and decline. Kalhana writes long after Parihasapura’s peak, preserving its memory even as its copper Buddha and golden Vishnu no longer stand.

panels.shot: close-up on scholarly hands turning pages of Rajatarangini and Xuanzang

dialogue.text: Xuanzang’s earlier record of mixed monasteries and temples, and Kalhana’s later chronicle of Parihasapura, together sketch Kashmir as a place where many sacred houses could stand under one sky.

panels.shot: final wide shot of the plateau at dusk with ghostly outlines of Buddha and Vishnu

dialogue.text: Parihasapura shows how a wise state can shelter more than one sacred path—not by erasing difference, but by placing different gods, teachers, and communities within the same shared city of stone.
